title: Building a schedule: critical path & Gantt charts
blurb: Build a schedule from the WBS, find the critical path and float, show it on a Gantt chart and keep it up to date.
question: A leisure centre is replacing its booking system. Staff training is running a week late, yet the project manager says go-live is safe. A week later the build slips by a few days and she immediately warns the sponsor that go-live will move. Why treat the two delays so differently?

teach.body: A schedule sets out the activities needed to deliver the scope, in a logical order, with durations, resources and dates. Once agreed it becomes the time baseline that progress is measured against. In plain English: it answers 'what happens when, in what order, and what is the earliest we can finish?' It is built from the WBS, so every piece of work in the scope appears in it, and it is kept up to date until the project closes.

teach.body: The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent activities through the project network. Because it is the longest, it sets the shortest possible duration of the whole project. Activities on it have zero float: any delay to one of them delays the end date, unless you recover the time elsewhere. Plain English: it is the chain of jobs with no slack, so it is where the project manager watches hardest.

teach.h: Larkhill Leisure Centre: new booking system
teach.caption: Requirements, Design, Build and Test form the critical path. Data migration and training each carry two weeks of float, so a short slip there does not move go-live.

teach.h: Float, negative float and near-critical paths
teach.body: Float is the time an activity can be delayed without delaying the project end date (total float). Free float is the delay possible without delaying the next activity. Negative float means the plan already cannot meet a required date: the project is forecast late. A near-critical path has only a little float, so a modest slip can make it the new critical path. That is why non-critical work still needs watching.

teach.text: The critical path is the LONGEST path through the network, not the shortest, and 'critical' does not mean 'most important' or 'most difficult'. It means zero float. A cheap, simple task can be critical; an expensive, high-profile one may have plenty of float.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Say how the schedule is built: activities from the WBS, sequenced by dependencies, durations estimated, resources added.
Define the critical path: the longest sequence of dependent activities, with zero float, setting the shortest project duration.
Explain float: delay that a non-critical activity can absorb without moving the end date.
Explain the Gantt chart: bars on a timeline that make the plan and progress easy to communicate, with milestones as control points.
Explain maintenance: update progress, re-forecast, re-check the critical path, and change the baseline only through change control.
Schedule: activities from the WBS, in logical order, with durations, resources and dates; once approved it is the time baseline.
Critical path: longest chain of dependent activities, zero float, sets the shortest possible duration.
Float lets non-critical work slip without moving the end date; negative float means the plan is already late.
Gantt chart: bars on a timeline, easy to communicate; milestones are zero-duration control points.
Keep the schedule live: progress, forecasts and the critical path can all change.

summary: You can now describe how a schedule is built from the WBS and maintained through the project, and explain the critical path, float and milestones. You can also say what a Gantt chart and a network diagram are each best for, and how scheduling differs in linear and iterative life cycles.

A.q: Which statement best describes the critical path of a project?
options: The shortest route from project start to finish
The longest sequence of dependent activities
The activities that carry the greatest cost
The activities the sponsor ranks as top priority
A.why: The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent activities through the network. Its length sets the shortest possible project duration, and its activities have zero float.

whyNot.0: It is the longest path, not the shortest: the longest chain is what limits how quickly the project can finish.
whyNot.2: Cost has nothing to do with it. An inexpensive activity can be critical.
whyNot.3: Criticality comes from the schedule logic and float, not from stakeholder priority.

A.q: A council IT project's data cleansing activity finishes four days late, yet the forecast end date does not change. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The activity had enough float to absorb it
The sponsor approved an extension in advance
Delays are only counted at decision gates
Data activities are never part of a schedule
A.why: A non-critical activity has float: time it can slip without delaying the end date. A four-day slip inside its float leaves the end date unchanged.

whyNot.1: An extension would move the end date. Here the end date stayed the same because float absorbed the delay.
whyNot.2: Delays affect the forecast whenever they happen; gates are review points, not the only time progress counts.
whyNot.3: Every piece of work in the WBS, including data work, belongs in the schedule.

A.q: A project manager wants the sponsor to see the plan and current progress at a glance. Which presentation is most suitable?
options: A network diagram showing every logical link
A risk register sorted by probability
A Gantt chart with bars against a timeline
A responsibility assignment matrix
A.why: A Gantt chart shows activities as bars on a calendar timeline, with milestones, so it is easy to communicate the plan and how far work has progressed.

whyNot.0: A network diagram is ideal for analysing logic and float, but it is harder for non-specialists to read at a glance.
whyNot.1: A risk register records risks, not the timing of activities.
whyNot.3: A RAM or RACI shows who is responsible for what, not when the work happens.

B.q: Which description best fits a milestone in a project schedule?
options: A long activity that spans more than one phase
A buffer of spare time held at the end of the plan
A task that has the most float in the network
A significant event or point with zero duration
B.why: A milestone marks a significant event, such as a gate or a key handover. It has no duration and acts as a control point for monitoring.

whyNot.0: Activities have duration; milestones do not.
whyNot.1: A buffer is a block of protective time, a critical chain idea, not a milestone.
whyNot.2: Float belongs to activities. A milestone is a point in time, not a task with slack.

B.q: Which tool is used to analyse the logical links between activities in order to calculate the critical path?
options: A product breakdown structure
A network diagram
A stakeholder map
A cost breakdown structure
B.why: A network diagram shows each activity and its dependencies, so the longest path and the float on every other activity can be worked out.

whyNot.0: A PBS breaks down the products to be delivered; it has no sequence or durations.
whyNot.2: A stakeholder map shows interest and influence, not activity logic.
whyNot.3: A CBS breaks down costs; it does not show the order of work.

B.q: A schedule review shows negative float on an activity leading to a contractual handover date. What does this tell the project manager?
options: The activity has spare time that can be released
The activity is no longer on the critical path
The current plan cannot meet the required date
The activity's duration estimate must be too long
B.why: Negative float means that, on the current plan, the required date cannot be met: the work is forecast to finish late. Recovery action or a change decision is needed.

whyNot.0: Spare time would be positive float. Negative float means time is missing, not available.
whyNot.1: Negative float usually sits on the most critical path of all, the one that is forecast late.
whyNot.3: It may be a genuine shortfall, not an estimating error. The cause needs investigating rather than assuming.

C.q: A project manager monitors only critical path activities. Several other paths are just a few days shorter. What is the main risk?
options: Critical activities will start to gain float
A near-critical path may become critical unseen
The Gantt chart will no longer show milestones
Non-critical work will need more resources
C.why: Near-critical paths have very little float. A modest slip can make one of them the new critical path, and if nobody is watching it the end date can move without warning.

whyNot.0: Watching the critical path does not give its activities float; they stay at zero unless the plan changes.
whyNot.2: What you monitor does not change how milestones are displayed.
whyNot.3: Narrow monitoring does not change the resources an activity needs. The risk is an undetected slip.

C.q: Which statement best describes scheduling in an iterative life cycle?
options: Every task is detailed and fixed at the start
Time boxes are fixed and scope flexes to fit them
Dates move whenever new features are requested
A critical path replaces any need for priorities
C.why: Iterative schedules are a series of fixed time boxes. Detail is planned for each time box, and if time is short, lower-priority scope is deferred rather than the date being moved.

whyNot.0: Full up-front detail is typical of a linear schedule, not an iterative one.
whyNot.2: The time box end date is fixed; scope, not the date, is what flexes.
whyNot.3: Iterative teams rely on prioritisation (such as MoSCoW) to decide what fits each time box.

C.q: A sponsor approves a change request adding a new reporting module to a project. What should happen to the schedule?
options: Keep the old baseline so progress looks consistent
Absorb the work silently within the existing float
Wait until closure and record the impact as a lesson
Update the plan and baseline so they stay accurate
C.why: Approved changes must be built into the plans and schedule, so the baseline remains a true reference for measuring progress and the critical path is re-checked.

whyNot.0: An out-of-date baseline makes progress reporting meaningless.
whyNot.1: New work may use up float or create a new critical path; it has to be scheduled visibly.
whyNot.2: Waiting until closure means the project is managed against a plan nobody is following.

reteach.title: Think of cooking a Sunday roast
reteach.question: Everything must reach the table at 1 pm. The joint needs two hours in the oven; the vegetables take 30 minutes. Which job decides when dinner is ready, and which have slack?

blocks.h: The longest chain sets the time
blocks.body: Defrost, season and roast the joint, then rest it: that chain takes longest, so it is your critical path. If the joint goes in late, dinner is late. Cooking the vegetables is a short chain: they could go on at 12.00 or 12.30 and still be ready. That wiggle room is float. Laying the table has loads of float. 'Serve at 1 pm' is a milestone: a moment, not a job.

blocks.h: Sunday lunch as a Gantt chart
blocks.caption: The joint's chain is critical. The vegetables and the table have float: they can slip without delaying lunch.

blocks.text: Speeding up the vegetables will not get lunch on the table sooner. Only shortening the critical chain (the joint) can do that.

explain.body: Start from the WBS so nothing in scope is missed. Turn work packages into activities, sequence them using their dependencies, estimate durations, add the resources each needs, then analyse the network for the critical path. Present it, agree it and baseline it.

test.q: Where should the activities in a new project schedule come from, so that no part of the scope is missed?
options: The work packages in the WBS
The previous project's lessons
The team's personal to-do lists
The organisation's risk register
test.why: The WBS breaks the whole scope into work packages, so deriving activities from it ensures all the agreed work is scheduled.

whyNot.1: Lessons learned help improve planning but do not define this project's scope.
whyNot.2: Personal lists are partial and unstructured, so work would be missed.
whyNot.3: The risk register lists uncertainties, not the full set of work to be done.

explain.body: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent activities, with zero float. Other activities have float: time they can slip without delaying the end date. Float can be used up, and a near-critical path can become critical.

test.q: Which TWO statements about float are correct? 1. It lets an activity slip without moving the end date. 2. Critical activities have the most of it. 3. It can be used up, making a path critical. 4. It is a budget held for known risks.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
test.why: Float is the slack a non-critical activity has before it delays the end date (1), and once it is used up that path can become critical (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: critical activities have zero float.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: critical activities have zero float, and money for known risks is contingency, not float.

explain.body: A Gantt chart lists activities down the side and shows each as a bar against a timeline. It is easy to read, shows overlaps and progress, and carries milestones as zero-duration diamonds. A simple Gantt chart may not make the logic between activities clear, which is why the network diagram is used for analysis.

test.q: Which is a recognised limitation of a simple Gantt chart?
options: It cannot show activities against time
It cannot display any milestones at all
It is too hard for sponsors to understand
It may not show the logic between tasks
test.why: Unless links are drawn in, a Gantt chart shows when things happen but not why: the dependencies are not obvious, so it is weaker for logic analysis than a network diagram.

whyNot.0: Showing activities against time is exactly what a Gantt chart does.
whyNot.1: Milestones are commonly shown on Gantt charts as diamonds.
whyNot.2: Ease of understanding is the Gantt chart's main strength.

explain.body: A schedule is maintained, not filed. Record actual progress, update forecasts, re-check which path is critical, report against the baseline, and feed approved changes into the plan through change control so the baseline stays accurate.

test.q: Why should a project manager re-check the critical path after each progress update?
options: Delays elsewhere can change which path is critical
The critical path must be changed every reporting period
Sponsors expect a new critical path at each meeting
Float is only calculated at the end of a project
test.why: Slips on non-critical or near-critical activities can use up their float and make a different path the longest. Re-checking keeps attention on the right activities.

whyNot.1: The critical path only changes if progress or plans change it; there is no rule to change it each period.
whyNot.2: The reason is control of the end date, not a reporting ritual.
whyNot.3: Float is worked out when the schedule is built and updated as work progresses.
